title: 5 storylines we’re excited about ahead of the Italian GP
excerpt:
The second half of the season is well and truly underway and the final two European rounds take place over a double-header that kicks off in Italy. With McLaren resurgent but plenty for the home fans to get excited about, there are sure to be a number of talking points when the paddock arrives in Monza.

Antonelli set for a home race penalty

Given the support Ferrari always receive at Monza, the Italian fans could find themselves slightly torn this weekend, as Kimi Antonelli arrives at his home race as the championship leader.

Rewind 12 months and it would have been a surprising prediction to suggest Antonelli would be 59 points clear in the standings in just his second season in Formula 1, even with the expectation that Mercedes would deliver a championship-contending car.

Yet as the Silver Arrows continue to prioritise the best approach to the season as a whole – rather than any individual race – Antonelli will face a tall order to secure victory in his home Grand Prix due to a planned power unit penalty.

Reliability issues mean Mercedes believe they won’t make it to the end of the season without taking a penalty with each car at some stage, and they also have the potential to upgrade the power unit through the FIA’s Advanced Development and Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) mechanism.

Whether it is a new specification that is introduced at Monza or not, the team have confirmed Antonelli will take a full new power unit and start towards the back of the grid.

“With Kimi, we're taking the full thing,” Toto Wolff said in Zandvoort. “Our calculations say that that's the best track to take it. Obviously, algorithms don't take their nationality into consideration. We're here to fight for a championship and not get the most PR.”

Wolff confirms Antonelli is set for grid penalty at Monza

Red Bull’s driver situation

The summer shutdown ended with an unexpected driver line-up change – albeit only a temporary one – at Red Bull, after Isack Hadjar injured his wrist ahead of the Dutch Grand Prix, ruling him out of the race weekend at Zandvoort.

Liam Lawson was promoted in his place, and impressed despite the lack of practice mileage on offer during the Sprint weekend. By Saturday’s Qualifying session, Lawson was able to get close to Max Verstappen and secured a spot alongside his team mate on the fourth row, before a solid run to seventh place behind the McLaren, Mercedes and Ferrari cars.

With Lawson at Red Bull, Yuki Tsunoda returned at Racing Bulls and also had a strong weekend, just missing out on points. So both proved to be strong replacements while Hadjar recovers.

It has not yet been confirmed if Hadjar will be fit to return this weekend at Monza, but if not then it is expected that Red Bull will stick with the Zandvoort line-ups, giving both Lawson and Tsunoda another chance to impress. While it will be a race on a very different type of circuit, they would have three practice sessions to help them build on top of their previous weekend’s experience.

Stability in the driver market

In the build-up to the Dutch Grand Prix weekend, three driver contracts were confirmed that suggested there will be little movement across the grid in 2027.

First up was Alex Albon remaining with Williams, shortly followed by his team mate Carlos Sainz also committing his future to the team and ensuring an unchanged driver line-up for James Vowles to work with next year.

Then came the big news of Max Verstappen extending his Red Bull stay until at least the end of 2030, as the Dutchman reaffirmed his intention to complete his whole career with the team.

Since leaving the Netherlands, there has been further confirmation of a driver retaining their seat, as Franco Colapinto’s strong season has been rewarded with another year at Alpine alongside Pierre Gasly.

As it stands, there have only been extensions and renewals confirmed – with Lando Norris and McLaren also committing long-term to each other – as the driver market has stabilised this year. Aston Martin are a team of interest as Fernando Alonso has yet to announce his plans for 2027, while there could potentially be movement at Haas and Racing Bulls.

Ollie Bearman is expected to continue with Haas, and Esteban Ocon’s recent form shows he is doing everything he can to remain alongside him, but both seats are currently still available.

Although unconfirmed at this stage, it would be a major surprise if Isack Hadjar and Arvid Lindblad don’t keep their seats at Red Bull and Racing Bulls respectively, while Lawson’s substitute appearance keeps him in the mix for another season despite the emergence of Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov.

Why Norris and McLaren have committed to each other for the long term

The Tifosi

Sure, Kimi Antonelli is leading the Drivers’ Championship, but you can still expect to see a sea of red at Monza as the Tifosi come out in force.

Although McLaren have won the past two races, Ferrari have been Mercedes’ closest challenger on average this season, with Lewis Hamilton sitting joint-second in the standings, 59 points adrift of Antonelli.

The expected penalty for Antonelli should only serve to increase Ferrari’s chances of fighting for victory at their home race, as they look to make inroads into Mercedes’ 87-point lead in the Constructors’ Championship.

Racing at Monza in front of such a passionate fanbase is always a sight to behold during the year, and if one of Hamilton or Charles Leclerc can deliver a win then the atmosphere underneath the iconic podium will be something particularly special.

Celebrating a legend

Aside from Ferrari’s own hopes of victory, they will be paying tribute to one of the most successful drivers in Formula 1 history this coming weekend.

Michael Schumacher won five of his seven drivers’ titles with Ferrari from 2000-2005, but 2026 marks 30 years since the legendary German joined the team, and 20 years since his final victory for the Scuderia – achieved at Monza as he announced his first retirement from the sport.

It took five years to taste championship success, but there were still three race wins in his first season in red back in 1996 – including at Monza – as Schumacher secured a victory in each of his 11 seasons with Ferrari.

The team have revealed special race suits that will be worn by Hamilton and Leclerc that feature Schumacher’s logo and the seven stars he used to carry on his helmet design to signify his seven world titles. Ferrari say this week’s tributes are inspired by Schumacher’s “impact on the racing world” and “his enduring mindset”.

title: Vowles admits he worried about losing both Sainz and Albon
excerpt:
James Vowles has admitted that he was concerned by the possibility of Williams losing both Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon amid the team’s struggles this season, and says the confirmation both drivers will be staying on for next year has seen a “weight lifted” off the factory.

The 2025 campaign saw the Grove-based outfit climb from their previous ninth in the championship to an impressive fifth, a run of form that included two podium finishes for Sainz.

Things have proven much more challenging for Williams in 2026, however, with the team back down to P9 after only scoring 11 points so far. Despite the difficulties, both Sainz and Albon were recently confirmed as staying with the squad into next season.

Speaking to the media during the Dutch Grand Prix weekend – days on from the announcements – Vowles was asked whether he had been worried about losing them.

“[I was] concerned about losing both, because they are World Championship-material drivers that deserve the opportunity to be fighting for podiums or more, and we haven't delivered that,” he explained.

“And more than that, we had a scope of where we were moving to. I think that there's no doubt if you sort of look to the outside – I hope there's no doubt – over the last few years, we've been slowly stepping forward with last year being a blip. I think [it was] too positive from where we were, but a step in the right direction.

“So for us to move backwards isn't just a surprise to the drivers, it's a surprise to everyone else, and that will always create risk that you lose them. What I'm thankful for is, the moment we had problems, they stood by our side.

“There wasn't finger pointing, it was actually, ‘tell me what I can do’, and they both came into the factory, spoke to the whole organisation and gave them a lift. Carlos did the same and Alex did the same this week once they re-signed.

“They wanted to make sure that they were here with the team. They want this to be a part of them, that is here on a turnaround of this organisation, and I'm thankful for that. But it's also an indication of what we've shown them in the back end of what's happened and what we're doing about it.”

Albon and Sainz explain why they have kept faith in Williams

Vowles went on to outline why retaining Sainz and Albon was “incredibly important” to him.

“[Reason number] one, it shows the outside world – I can't tell you everything that's going on behind the scenes, but I can tell them, and if they are re-signing it will give you an indication that there's a lot of change ongoing and they believe in what the future looks like.

“And that belief is incredibly important, whether it's for team members or for anyone in the outside world.

“Number two, that consistency is important because the team is really maturing and changing and, as much as you can keep consistent, especially in a driver line-up, it becomes desperately important in order to keep building on that.

“Probably the best way to summarise it to you is [that in] the factory, there's a weight lifted off it this week as the result of it and I've seen them move forward at a much faster pace as a result, so the belief is real and tangible.”

With Albon’s re-signing publicly confirmed first before Sainz’s followed one day later, Vowles also suggested that there was a reason behind the separate announcements.

“For me, and for the drivers, it was important to state that they are different stories and different timings,” the Team Principal said.

“Also, it helped me because Alex was in the simulator on Tuesday and Carlos on Wednesday. I was able to show them to the team and I didn't have them both on the same day at the same time!

“But for me, they're different journeys. Alex has been here since 2022. He has dedicated so much of his life to this project and he wants it to be successful, and I think that's one message in its own right.

“With Carlos, what he needed was to be demonstrated what's happening behind the scenes and he wanted to then commit into the long term, and it's a very different set of arrangements that we have between the two of them. I think the messaging is no different though.

“We all have unfinished business. Our goal is to have Alex and Carlos by our side for many years to come. We have to do work on our side in order to make sure we are stepping up, irrespective of our drivers. The drivers are not the limitation to us at the moment. We are.

“We have to fix that, and quickly, for us more than anything else. But the announcements of the drivers will show you that there's belief in the project for the long term, and that individuals, even the ones that have been here since ‘22, can see the change and want to be a part of it.”

title: F1 NATION: Will Antonelli or Ferrari be home heroes at Monza?
excerpt:
Lando Norris is riding a wave of impressive form having taken back-to-back victories in the last two Grands Prix.

The reigning World Champion claimed wins either side of the Formula 1 summer break at the Hungaroring and then at Zandvoort.

But next up is a very different type of challenge, as the F1 teams and drivers head to Monza for this weekend's Italian Grand Prix.

Will the low downforce Temple of Speed circuit expose McLaren's weaknesses? Or could Norris really turbo-charge his title challenge by making it three wins in a row?

He might be aided in his quest by the fact that championship leader Kimi Antonelli will be taking a grid penalty at his home race, so if the Italian is going to claim a seventh Grand Prix win of the season, he's going to have to fight his way up the order to do it.

The partisan home crowd will of course be cheering on Ferrari, but after going two races without a podium for the first time this season, can the Scuderia find form again and give the Tifosi a race to remember?

And after crashing on the opening lap at his home race last time out, can Max Verstappen bounce back with a strong result at a track where he's won three of the last four Grands Prix?

Tom Clarkson is joined by former Renault F1 driver Jolyon Palmer and IndyCar winner James Hinchcliffe to discuss all that and plenty more in this week's F1 Nation podcast.

The team have a full preview of this weekend's Grand Prix, plus there's reaction to Franco Colapinto extending his contract with Alpine for 2027 – and the team remember when Jolyon upset Fernando Alonso at Monza.

title: What time is the 2026 Italian GP and how can I watch it?
excerpt:
The 2026 Formula 1 season continues this weekend with the Italian Grand Prix, with Monza set to host Round 13 – and here are the global start times for Sunday’s race.

A strong weekend for McLaren’s Lando Norris in the Netherlands indicated that the fight at the top is heating up, with the reigning World Champion clinching back-to-back victories for the first time in 2026. He’s still got a significant deficit to championship leader Kimi Antonelli, who holds a 59-point lead over both his team mate George Russell and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton.

Head to the RACE HUB or scroll down for more on how and when you can watch the action, along with the global start times for each session.

What time is the 2026 Italian Grand Prix?

The weekend will begin with FP1 on Friday, 4 September at 1230 local time, followed by FP2 at 1600.

A final hour of practice takes place at 1230 on Saturday, 5 September before the drivers compete for the best grid spots in Qualifying at 1600. Lastly, the Grand Prix starts at 1500 on Sunday, 6 September.

Check out the image below to find all the global start times for Sunday’s race.

How can I watch the 2026 Italian Grand Prix?

You can enjoy coverage from every session live on F1 TV Pro (available in selected countries), which brings fans closer to the action via exclusive features like onboard cameras on all 22 of the drivers’ cars, and access to both Pre-Race and Post-Race Shows.

F1 TV Pro can be streamed easily via Apple TV, Chromecast Generation 2 and above, Android TV, Google TV, Amazon Fire TV, and Roku. F1 TV Pro is free of ad breaks and available with commentary in six languages.

Fans can also watch via F1 TV Premium, a premier service that invites fans to step into the heart of the action with the ability to watch races in 4K Ultra HD/HDR on up to six different devices, as well as a personalised Multiview feature available on select devices with 26 different feeds to choose from.

Viewers can watch every F1 Grand Prix, F1 Sprint, Qualifying and practice session live in 4K Ultra HD/HDR at home, with F2, F3, F1 ACADEMY and Porsche Supercup sessions also available to watch live on the platform.

Alternatively, live timing will be available on F1.com and the F1 app across every session during the Grand Prix weekend.

Where is the 2026 Italian Grand Prix taking place?

The Italian Grand Prix will be held at the Autodromo Nazionale Monza, the oldest circuit on the calendar. Originally constructed in 1922, it became the world’s third purpose-built race track and was part of the inaugural F1 season in 1950.

It has hosted nearly every Italian Grand Prix since, with the exception of the 1980 event when the venue underwent refurbishment, and is loved for its history, remarkable high speeds and the passionate Tifosi.

They were delighted by Charles Leclerc's fairytale victories in Monza in 2019 and 2024, but it’s Hamilton and Michael Schumacher who jointly hold the record of five wins.

What is the weather forecast in Italy?

Conditions are expected to be warm and sunny, with temperatures reaching 30 Celsius across all three days of track action and minimal chance of rain in the region.

When can I watch F2 and F3 during the 2026 Dutch Grand Prix weekend?

Formula 2 returns to action this weekend, with Nikola Tsolov seeking to extend his 20-point lead over Gabriele Mini in the championship.

Free Practice will start proceedings at 1000 local time on Friday, September 4, followed by Qualifying at 1455.

The Sprint Race, which sees the top 10 finishers from Qualifying reversed, will take place at 1415 on Saturday, September 5 before the lights go out for the Feature Race at 0945 on Sunday, September 6.

F3 will also contest the penultimate round of the season at Monza as Freddie Slater and Ugo Ugochukwu continue to battle for the title. The weekend will begin with Free Practice at 0855 on Friday, September 4, with the field divided into two groups for Qualifying A at 1400 and Qualifying B at 1420.

The top 12 qualifiers will be reversed for the Sprint Race at 0930 on Saturday, September 5, and the Feature Race will conclude the weekend at 0815 on Sunday, September 6.

title: Why Jack Doohan values childhood neighbour Michael Schumacher
excerpt:
Not many people can say they grew up with a seven-time F1 World Champion as their neighbour, but Haas reserve Jack Doohan can. Not only was Michael Schumacher close friends with Doohan’s father Mick – himself a five-time World Champion on two wheels – but he gifted the young Jack his first go-kart, a moment that helped spark his own journey in motorsport.

In our latest edition of F1 Icons, Doohan explains why Schumacher is his idol in the sport and how that admiration stems from much more than performances and titles…

My father and Michael Schumacher were very close friends. After 1994 they both won their first world championships and somehow were neighbours – one winning on two wheels and one on four wheels. The relationship started there and all my very early years were crossed over with Michael.

I would spend time around the house so, on four wheels, Michael has never been out of the equation for being my idol. I also received my first go-kart from him – for me and my sister – and that was really the start to getting where I am now.

Even if we don’t touch further on what he’s done in the sport, or how successful his F1 story is, I’m incredibly grateful for having such a close relationship with him.

The magnitude of him as an athlete definitely didn’t hit early on. I was a three, five, seven-year-old kid coming home from school and he was just with my father – whatever it might be. When these people are close to you, they’re just another good human like we all are. That’s the basis that gets lost sometimes in the F1 paddock.

At the end of the day, drivers are just normal people. I always say that – apart from being a performer, which essentially we are right? Athlete performers, no different to the circus!

You’re just another Joe Blow. You’ve got the same routine, you wake up, you have your coffee, you do your stuff, you go to work and you come back home.

Hall of Fame: Michael Schumacher

I always wanted to stick so true to those values of being no different to anyone else no matter where on the schedule you are in life. With Michael, I was sort of embedded in that and I really wanted to carry those values in myself.

On track he carried himself with confidence. Obviously, he had good people around him, but he had the right amount of aggressiveness. His calculated tolerance was very assertive and the way he placed the car on track, what he would do with it on track, was extremely strong.

He was always there, you know? Even when things weren’t flowing – whether it be gearbox issues or failures – and he was very, very passionate on and off the track from what I’ve heard from my father.

So, the values are very similar. Especially correlating that between other drivers that my father knew around that time compared to Michael, and hearing the lengths and extent that he worked away from the track, it’s clear to see why he was as successful as he was.

The standouts were being physically fit and being mentally fit. Both him and my dad, instead of getting two hours of work done and saying, ‘I did my deed’ they were consistently going tail for tail and pushing one another. They weren’t just doing what was needed and then moving on.

It's difficult to put his legacy into words, right? And it's going to vary from person to person.

It really comes down to statistics. You can be the most successful Formula 1 driver of all time because in the 1960s, you might have jumped in for one race and won. On a spreadsheet they might have a 100% success rate but are you better than Lewis Hamilton, Michael Schumacher or Sebastian Vettel?

That’s an argument to be said because there will be different perspectives on statistics. Arguing what’s going to be right or wrong really varies from person to person.

For me, regardless of winning seven World Championships over two different decades – with different machinery and different types of vehicles – it’s incredibly inspiring to keep so strong for so long. And then to rejoin in a different time again with a new team fresh off the bat.

There are multiple aspects to praise him, but for me there is so much more beyond his performances inside the car that make Michael Schumacher my F1 idol.

title: The car I loved and the car I loathed – with Nigel Mansell
excerpt:
Nigel Mansell drove a wide range of cars across his F1 career, from Lotus machines he struggled to qualify in to the Williams FW14B with which he ultimately claimed the Drivers’ World Championship title.

But what were the standout designs that he loved and loathed in equal measure? For a new F1.com series, we put those questions to him. Read on to discover his choices, as well as to learn more about each car...

The car Mansell loved: Williams FW11B

“The car I really loved more than anything was the FW11B. It was the fastest car, I think, ever, or [the most] powerful car ever to be developed in F1, with 1,500 horsepower using a Qualifying tyre. That blew your mind.

"Martin Brundle was absolutely spot on: it was a car that wanted to kill you on every corner. So that car… I loved it. I hated it at the same time, because it was trying to kill you! But when you drove that, it was a monster – a monster. You knew when you got out and you were in one piece that you’d done half a decent job.”

F1 technical expert Mark Hughes says…

“The Williams FW11B was the 1987 low-line version of the 1986 FW11. Because the fuel limit had been reduced from 220 litres to 195 in the regulations, the smaller tank allowed the car to be packaged accordingly. There were suspension changes, too, but essentially this was the same concept as before and powered by Honda’s hugely powerful RA167E, which got around the 4-bar turbo boost limit regulated for ’87 to be even more powerful than the unrestricted ’86 engine.”

The car(s) Mansell loathed: Lotus 81B and Lotus 92

“I think the car I really didn’t enjoy at all for a period of time, and loathed, was the first active Lotus car, [the 92], when we were developing that. It was throwing you off the circuit and causing you to have accidents when you were going in a straight line. That was a terrible experience to go through.

“The other car, I think, was the first Lotus that I drove, [the 81B], to try and qualify in a Grand Prix. It was seven inches longer than the normal Lotus car that we were developing, and it wouldn’t turn quickly, because it was too long. It was something that we were trying, but I didn’t enjoy that one either!”

F1 technical expert Mark Hughes says…

“The Lotus 92 was a stop-gap car used by Mansell for the first half of the 1983 season. It initially featured active suspension (the first ever in F1), but this was abandoned after two races because of its unreliability and extra weight. This was Team Lotus’ first season with turbo engines (from Renault) and Lotus had built an entirely different car – the 93T – around that engine. However, Renault could not initially supply enough engines for two cars and so another car had to be built to take the existing non-turbo Cosworth DFV engine. This was the 92 model which Mansell so disliked, especially in active form. The 93T proved uncompetitive and both it and the 92 were replaced by the turbo-powered 94T from the British Grand Prix onwards.

“The Lotus 81B of 1980 was a longer wheelbase version of the original 81. A ground effect car, the 81 struggled in the midfield and it was felt that part of its aerodynamic shortfall was that there was too small a gap between the rear face of the engine and the diffuser, hence a longer wheelbase version was created. This simply created a car with a great reluctance to turn in and was even less competitive than the standard car.”

title: Antonelli interview: The title fight and his Monza mindset
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli is living his best life right now. It's the Italian's second season in Formula 1 and he sits on top of the Drivers' Championship with a 59-point lead over his team mate George Russell and Lewis Hamilton, the seven-time World Champion whom he replaced at Mercedes in 2025.

Seven F1 Grands Prix have been won by teenagers and Antonelli has won six of them (four-time World Champion Max Verstappen won the other). He took his first pole in China this year and converted that into his first Grand Prix victory. The now 20-year-old went on a run of five wins on the bounce, which included dominating on the streets of Monte Carlo to win the Monaco Grand Prix.

Antonelli has hardly put a foot wrong all year, making the most of a very fast Mercedes and outperforming his more experienced team mate Russell. Even on the weekends when a little error creeps in or he struggles to find the limit, Antonelli has managed to find a way to rescue a strong result – like third in Hungary before the break and second in Zandvoort after.

title: Why Norris has committed to McLaren for the long term
excerpt:
Michael Jordan and Scottie Pippen, Xavi and Andres Iniesta, Lando Norris and McLaren – there are just some sporting partnerships that are meant to be.

On Saturday, it was announced that the latter will be staying together for the foreseeable future with Norris signing a fresh deal that'll keep him at McLaren until at least the end of 2030.

When Zak Brown got to know a young aspiring racer called Lando Norris, very quickly he formed the opinion that the Briton was World Championship material.

Brown was proved right last year as the 26-year-old fended off team mate Oscar Piastri and a charging Max Verstappen to clinch the Drivers' World Championship crown.

That title success came in year nine of their time together, which began with Norris walking through the doors of the McLaren Technology Centre (MTC) in Woking in 2017 as a 17-year-old to sign a contract to become test and development driver.

Norris was an instant hit with McLaren and McLaren was an instant hit with Norris. They've grown up together, gone through tough times together and enjoyed success together. They've got each other's respective backs.

That's the kind of environment that Norris thrives in. As he told me in his first interview since the news broke, he's with the people that he wants to be with and "for me, that's calming".

Norris' previous contract ran until at least the end of 2027, so there was no rush to get a new deal done, not least because both Brown and Norris knew they were happy and wanted to continue. So why do another deal already?

Well, following his World Championship victory last year – McLaren's first Drivers' World Championship trophy since Lewis Hamilton triumphed in 2008 – it was always the plan to sit down and discuss extending and improving their arrangement.

Norris signs new McLaren deal until end of 2030

So, in the last few months, they zeroed in on the new terms with both sides sure that, not only did they want to continue beyond 2027, but they wanted to commit for the long-term, which in this case is at least the next four years.

The deal is understood to be a proper commitment from both sides and a clear intention to see it through, rather than a deal that has clauses that could allow one or the other to escape each year.

For Norris, he was keen to do a long-term deal to give him and those around him stability and prevent the persistent rumours about his future floating around and acting as a distraction.

Knowing he'll be at McLaren untll at least the end of 2030, when he'll be 31, also means he can knuckle down and focus on working with his team to add to his win and World Championship tally.

He also believes McLaren have what it takes to win. He believes Brown and Team Principal Andrea Stella are "incredible" leaders and feels the team of people who work with him are the best in the business and are all working in the right direction to bring success. So there really was no reason to change.

For McLaren, they have seen Norris grow from a rising star to a World Champion and were there every step of the way, from signing his first contract and taking his first pole, to sealing his first Grand Prix win and taking the title.

They know what they've got – and they know what he's worth – so understandably, they don't want to let him go.

Signing such an impressive deal that locks him down for at least another four years gives certainty to their shareholders and partners and wards off any admirers – of which there are many – elsewhere in the pit lane.

The driver market could get very spicy in 2028, so locking Norris down early doors sets out their stall and sends a warning signal to rivals.

Trust and belief in each other. Those factors formed the foundations of Norris and McLaren's relationship back in 2017 and, a decade on, they remain the cornerstones.

With team mate Piastri signed up until the end of 2028 – and both sides believed to be very happy with their relationship – McLaren are well set for the future as they battle to create a papaya-coloured dynasty in the years ahead.

title: Norris opens up on why he sees his future at McLaren
excerpt:
Lando Norris is beaming. This isn't uncommon as it's pretty much his baseline, but the Briton's smile and chirpiness is noticeably even brighter when we meet on the uber-cool boulevard of the McLaren Technology Centre for a chat.

This is because Norris is here to talk about a huge new deal that will keep him at McLaren until at least the end of 2030. Come the end of that term, he'll have been with the team for 12 years, equaling the record stint countryman Lewis Hamilton had with Mercedes.

It's an extraordinary show of faith in McLaren, with the British team holding the same belief in Norris. And given how perfect Norris and McLaren seem for each other, it's perhaps no surprise that he's chosen to extend his stay with a team where he feels at home.

"I'm very, very excited," he says in his first interview since the news was announced. "McLaren's been my home since the very, very beginning of my career in Formula 1 and I want it to stay that way for as long as possible. We've had a great few years and I'm confident we can achieve that many more times. So I want to stay."

Norris began his F1 journey with McLaren, starting as a test and developing driver, before stepping up as a reserve. He got the nod for a race seat in 2019, racing alongside Carlos Sainz, and went on to take his first podium in Austria 2020 and first pole in Russia 2021.

His first win came in Miami 2024, his first Monaco triumph in 2025 and his first Grand Prix victory on home soil followed that year when he won at Silverstone. He of course would go on to pick up his first World Championship and McLaren's first drivers' title since 2008.

They've seen it all together but they're not done yet. Why change what isn't broken? Especially when you can confirm your long-term future and give yourself some stability.

"I know for a good amount more years that I'm comfortable in terms of I've got a job and I’m where I want to be, and with the people that I want to be with, and for me that's calming," he says. "I can focus on a job I need to do and as a team we can also focus on the job that we want to do."

He adds: "You can always see results as most important and 99% of the time I think they are, but I would say there's leeway, there's leverage in terms of just the fact I'm with the people that I want to be with, people that I enjoy spending my career with.

Norris signs new McLaren deal until end of 2030

"I don't want to be bouncing around teams and doing different things. I want be where I'm happy and, even when we weren't winning, I was also happy to be part of McLaren.

"I think something I always know for my future is I want results of course – the team know that just as much as anyone – but I also just want to be wherever I'm most happy and even if we're not winning like the beginning of this year, it's not like I want to change team.

"I'm still very happy with who I am with and happy to kind of fight through whatever we have coming up."

'I don’t want to distract my team'

Fighting back McLaren are. After a slow start, which included McLaren failing to take the start in the opener in Australia and both failing to start at the following race in China, the reigning World Champions are fighting back.

An upgrade in Hungary before the break hauled them into contention and opened the door for Norris to secure his and the team's first victory of the season. That package was completed with more parts after the break in Zandvoort, with Norris taking pole and a second successive victory.

He's still someway off in the championship fight, as he sits 83 points behind leader Kimi Antonelli, but he and McLaren have the momentum – and if last year is anything to go by (when Max Verstappen sliced through a 104-point deficit to force a title decider in Abu Dhabi) Norris is very much in with a chance of defending his title.

That response is just what Norris knows McLaren are capable of, but that form didn't trigger this renewal. Those chats had been in the diary since he won the world title in Abu Dhabi last year.

Norris knew he wanted to stay and McLaren knew they wanted to keep them. To warn off admirers from elsewhere on the grid and to stamp out any ambiguity about his future, they were both keen to extend.

Drivers' Championship after Zandvoort

"It's a continuation of my last [contract]," he says. "We just want to be able to focus on doing our best job, to extract performance, to get the most out of everyone and focus on the importance that we do not get caught up in the mess of everyone else deciding contracts.

"I don’t want to distract my team, I don't want to distract the guys and girls here that are here to give me the best car possible and for me to do the best job for them.

"We want to focus on our jobs and not think about all the noise that goes on in the sidelines. So for me it's 'guys I'm here to stay. I want to be with you for a long time' and it gives them a good boost, gives me a good boost and together it means we can just focus."

'I want to make this my home'

Norris also believes in the set-up McLaren have, led by CEO Zak Brown and Team Principal Andrea Stella. "Zak is a very good leader, he's a very good boss," says Norris.

"As much as we get on and we just, we love racing, we want to win together, we enjoy golf and things, he is still my boss so he still gives me a kick whenever I do something wrong or if I'm not doing something well enough.

"That's always what I want – someone that's honest and who gives me the brutal truth no matter what it is and that something that's very important to me.

"At the same time I have that very much so with Andrea, and Andrea is for me – and of course I'm biased and this is the only place I've been – but we have had a few different team principals and he is most certainly the most influential over the team.

"He is an incredible leader, someone who knows how to bring a group of people together and also knows how to lead individuals such as me in terms of how I can go out and increase my performance every day and be a better person.

"So, even if I could change anything with where I am now, I wouldn't and I think that's the perfect reason."

Will Norris, who will be 31 when this next deal expires, ever leave McLaren? There's a very good chance he won't.

"I want to make this my home," says the Briton, who holds the record for the most starts for McLaren. "I want it to be the place that I am at for a very, very long time and maybe even forever.

"There are more nice things that just allow me to work better here and live better here, and that's an amazing thing."

title: Carlos Sainz concedes mental 'worry' before agreeing fresh Williams deal
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz has conceded that he was "worried" before agreeing to renew his contract with Williams, due to wanting to ensure its current poor season is not replicated.

After a remarkable opening campaign with Williams last season, which saw the Spaniard feature on the podium, 2026 has been a staggering wake-up call.

Williams missed the pre-season shakedown in Barcelona and had a significant weight issue, hurting the Grove-based outfit throughout the year so far.

It has left Sainz frustrated and disappointed, having expected so much better from the start of the new power unit regulations, leading to speculation that he could depart.

However, ahead of this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix, it was confirmed by the British outfit that Sainz had signed a new multi-year deal, with him not wanting to leave at the first obstacle.

Asked if he needed convincing to renew his Williams deal, Sainz told select media, including RacingNews365: "No, because in a way, I think you guys know me by now. I don't think it's part of my character to jump ships when the situation is also at its worst.

"I think I told everyone also how committed I am to this project two years ago, how excited I was about it, and the first time there is a bump on the road, a big bump, probably bigger than anyone could have imagined after the podiums of last year.

"I don't think it's part of me, my way of being, my character to jump ships at the first possible opportunity. So I think, in the back of my head, I always wanted to renew, but I was obviously worried, concerned that we need to make sure this doesn't happen again.

"And I obviously had to go back to everyone and understand where we are, where we're planning to go, and how this has affected our plans."

title: Valtteri Bottas clarifies F1 future after surprise Cadillac sacking
excerpt:
Valtteri Bottas has clarified that he has no concerns in the "near future" about retaining his Cadillac F1 race seat after the surprise sacking of Graeme Lowdon.

Lowdon was relieved of his duties during F1's summer break by CEO Dan Towriss, with former Alpine technical chief Marcin Budkowski appointed as his replacement.

Cadillac has failed to score a point thus far during its debut F1 season, with its best result being Bottas's 13th in China as the team has battled reliability issues throughout the European leg of the campaign, including issues with the brakes catching fire and a suspension failure for team-mate Sergio Perez in Canada.

Bottas was regarded as a Lowdon signing, with the former team boss putting on an extraordinary press briefing to two media outlets, including RacingNews365, around the Monaco GP when rumours swirled that Bottas would be dropped, with Lowdon defending his driver.

Under the new leadership, Bottas has confirmed that he has no concerns over his immediate future in seeing out the season.

"Not in the near future, no," Bottas replied to media, including RacingNews365, when asked if he had any concerns about his future.

"I'm still all set, obviously, for next year. But then eventually we're going to talk about what is happening beyond 2027, but that's not yet."

When then asked about Lowdon's departure, Bottas explained that he felt "time would tell" if it was the right decision, but that "something needed to change."

"I respect [the decision] and like with any change, time will always tell what change is good and what change is bad," Bottas said.

"I can't predict the future, and I don't know Marcin that well yet. I haven't worked with him in the past, and I've worked with Graeme quite a bit in the past, and it is just a personal relationship, but time will tell.

"I think that something needed to change; some of the issues we've had have been dragging along, but I didn't maybe expect such a big change.

"I was maybe expecting more stuff happening at the factory, but it is one of those things.

"We as drivers don't see what needs to be changed sometimes when it comes to these things, because we're obviously very focused on the driving and performance and giving our feedback.

"We are not the people who structure the team; that is not our job."

title: George Russell is building 'toolbox of experience' to re-engage after F1 title woes
excerpt:
George Russell has described how the "toolbox of experience" he has developed during his 2026 F1 title woes will be used in good stead in future battles.

After 12 races of the season, the Briton is 59 points behind team-mate Kimi Antonelli in the title race, with the Italian also having the buffer of six grand prix wins to Russell's two.

Despite winning the season-opener in Australia, Russell has struggled to get on top of the W17 at times, with an issue in his driving style affecting performances, before power unit software issues affected his British and Belgian GP weekends.

After a tough first half of the season, Russell came back with a dominant Sprint victory in the Dutch GP weekend, and qualified second for the main grand prix, and looked set to take further points out of Antonelli, having already reduced his deficit by three with the win.

In the grand prix, Antonelli finished second to Russell's third, meaning the gap exiting the weekend was the same 59 points as it was entering it, leaving Russell with one fewer weekend to reel in his team-mate.

However, Russell believes that he has made a breakthrough in his driving style and understanding with the car, and that the tough experiences he has gone through in 2026, will be added to the "toolbox of experience" he hopes to draw upon in the remainder of this campaign, and in the future.

"I think the truth is, obviously Kimi’s been doing an amazing job this season, and clearly the two of us have quite different driving styles," Russell observed to media, including RacingNews365.

"That was apparent last year, and it is really working well for him with this car and these tyres, and I'm just trying to implement something similar into my driving style.

"I kind of describe it as, like, if you change your golf swing, you’ll probably take half a step back before making those improvements, and I think the break just allowed me to put those learnings into the back of my mind, come [to the Dutch GP] and not fixate on what I want to try and achieve with the car and the tyres, but knowing in the back of my head what I need to achieve and just drive more freely.

"I’m really, really proud of that because it’s just sort of building that toolbox of experience for me that’s going to allow me to be even better in the years to come.

"Who knows, maybe next year the technique is totally different again. That’s the beauty and challenge of Formula 1. Every year it’s different.

"I’m just going to take it race by race. I’m not going to come away from [the Zandvoort weekend] and say all issues are resolved. I do think I made some big changes going into the Barcelona weekend, and I had some good races in Barcelona and Austria.

"Then Silverstone and Spa, we had the PU issue, and Budapest was just not a competitive weekend on my side. So, I think it just hasn’t been a clean run this season.

"It has not been a clean season whatsoever with all of the issues that we’ve had. But I just feel, I think after the break, I just feel way more relaxed. I don’t feel like I’ve got anything to lose.

"The pressure’s off. I’m just going to go out, enjoy it, and I don’t even really feel in a fight.

"It’s not mine to lose; it’s mine to gain. So that’s the mentality I’ve got, and I feel it’s going to help me. I’m just enjoying driving."

title: Fernando Alonso makes firm Aston Martin declaration in retirement evaluation
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso insists that he will be with Aston Martin "in one role or another", even if he decides to retire from racing in F1.

The two-time champion, who holds a record total of 437 starts in the series, is currently evaluating whether to extend his career into a 24th season in 2027, or to call it quits at the end of what would be his fourth season with Aston Martin.

Following the poor start to the season, there have been flashes of improvement from the team and its Honda engine supplier, with Alonso claiming a season-best result of ninth in the Dutch Grand Prix last time out, tripling his points haul in the season to three from one.

Whilst the "ultimate dream" for Alonso is to join Sir Jack Brabham, Sir Jackie Stewart, Niki Lauda, Nelson Piquet, and Ayrton Senna as a three-time F1 world champion, he has conceded that the team is a "very long" way from being able to fight for the title, and that "maybe I am not behind the wheel" when it happens.

However, Alonso has declared that in whatever position, he will be with Aston Martin "for the long term" as it tries to scale title summit.

"I've said many times, the regulations are what it is. It's not the best, the most fun cars to drive, but still, my life and Formula 1 have been... it will always be my life, and my heart is here," Alonso told media, including RacingNews365.

"I will be with this team in one role or in another for the long term, so it's not about myself or about who is driving next year, or if I'm driving next year or three more years. I don't know.

"It's sitting with Lawrence [Stroll] and with Adrian [Newey], and if the needs for the team are for me to drive, I will consider it. I will be happy if I can be more valuable in another position. I will consider it, and I will be happy as well, but I need to drive something.

"That's something for sure. I need to race. I need to feel the adrenaline. I'm a competitor, and I have other challenges in my head. As I've said many times, to win the Dakar one day or to try again the Indy 500, or whatever is coming next, and also winning in Formula 1 a third world championship, which will obviously be the ultimate dream.

"Is that possible? I don't know how long it will take to achieve that performance for this team; it's going to be a very long time.

"Maybe I'm not behind the wheel, but that's something that is all in my head."

title: Ralf Schumacher set for surgery after jet ski accident
excerpt:
Former F1 driver Ralf Schumacher is set to undergo a surgical procedure after a jet ski accident.

The incident occurred during a live TV event, Stefan Raab's celebrity jet ski world championship in Duisburg.

In the individual competition, Schumacher made it to the final but missed out on the win before attention turned to the team tournament.

Schumacher participated alongside host Raab, but things did not go according to plan as they capsized at a buoy, causing both to fall off.

The jet ski capsized again just moments later when Schumacher powered away as Raab hadn't fully climbed back on yet.

As Schumacher attempted to get back on again, it was clear that he was in pain, and he later explained to RTL: "My shoulder was dislocated when I tried to turn the jet ski around so quickly.”

After his shoulder was put back in place, an X-ray revealed that he had a minor break which will require surgery.

However, Schumacher, who works for Sky Germany as an F1 pundit, is expecting to be present in Monza this weekend for the Italian Grand Prix.

"It was only a shoulder dislocation, or a dislocated shoulder, but unfortunately a piece of bone broke off as well," Schumacher said.

"The operation will be over quickly and then I should be back in Monza as well. I only have to hold my microphone with my left hand!"

title: Ferrari voice key F1 concern over end-of-season doubt
excerpt:
Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur has highlighted a key area of concern hanging over F1 as the wait continues to discover how the end of the season will unfold.

Due to the ongoing war between the United States and Iran in the Middle East, doubt shrouds the final two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

F1 CEO and president Stefano Domenicali has previously stated that no decision on those two races will be made before the middle of September. It has even been suggested such a call could be delayed until the start of October.

F1, it seems, is willing to wait as long as possible before confirming whether two of its most lucrative races of the campaign will be staged.

Domenicali has also stated that if the two grands prix are cancelled, then the season will end with a race in Europe - believed to be Imola - and not in Las Vegas.

Vasseur feels that from a cost cap perspective, the teams need to know sooner rather than later whether they will be heading to Qatar and Abu Dhabi, as it will then allow them to direct considerable financial resources needed for those events elsewhere.

Initially dismissing power unit component concerns, in trying to manage the systems for 22 or 23 races, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365, Vasseur said: "Cost cap could be a trickier point because the cost of going to Abu Dhabi and Qatar to do two races is huge.

"If we don't go there, perhaps you can spend elsewhere, in development or whatever. It's true for us, but it's true for everybody. At some stage we will have to take a decision.

"For everybody, for logistics reasons, collectively we will have to decide by September because we will have to send the kits to the Middle East, and we won't be able to postpone any more on this.

"It will probably be enough to manage the last six or seven races after September."

Next up for Vasseur and Ferrari is the Scuderia's home Italian Grand Prix at Monza on September 6.

title: Mercedes name 'priority decision' key to Kimi Antonelli-George Russell team order
excerpt:
Mercedes has explained how its focus on delivering the "priority" of giving its lead car the ability to attack was central to the team order delivered to George Russell in the Dutch Grand Prix.

Under a virtual safety car for Esteban Ocon's stricken Haas, Mercedes elected to pit Kimi Antonelli from second at Zandvoort, with team-mate George Russell moving up to second place with the Italian slotting in behind on fresher tyres.

Shortly after the restart, Russell was asked to cede position to Antonelli to allow him to regain second place and try to hunt down leader Lando Norris for the race victory. A complicating factor for Russell is that in letting Antonelli past, he would suffer a negative six-point swing in the championship fight, but ultimately let his team-mate go.

Russell was then engaged in a fierce battle with the Ferraris for third place, and successfully held on for the podium, aided in part by a further late VSC, but fell to 59 points behind Antonelli - effectively wiping out the three points he had gained back in his Sprint win, and leaving him the same number of points behind the Italian as he was coming into the weekend.

Reflecting on the order, deputy team principal Bradley Lord explained how a pre-race team meeting made clear that such action might be taken, and how the "priority" was to give the lead car on the day, Antonelli, the chance to win the race.

"No," Lord explained when asked if there was any concern over how Russell would react to the order.

"Because of the early red flag and the delayed schedule, we held the full debrief on Monday rather than immediately after the race. George naturally questioned the instruction when he first received it, but he understood the wider picture.

"Kimi had taken the opportunity for a free stop under the virtual safety car. Had George made the same stop, he would have dropped behind a Ferrari and surrendered the podium position.

"We had also been very clear in the Sunday morning strategy meeting that the field was too close for our drivers to lose time fighting one another. That discussion provided the basis for the decision.

"Had the circumstances been reversed, we would have acted in exactly the same way. The priority was to give the car in second the best chance of attacking, while giving the car in third clear air and the best opportunity to defend its position."

Trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin then offered a response to whether it was considered to have Antonelli drop back once it was clear he wouldn't catch Norris to give Russell access to the overtake mode boost in power to defend from the charging Ferraris of Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc in the fight for third.

"We discussed it. The gain was around two tenths of a second, principally on the straight, which was also where George was most vulnerable," said Shovlin.

"There was a concern that trying something we had not rehearsed could cause the cars to become entangled. Because the lap-time gain was not enormous, we decided it was better for Kimi to move ahead cleanly and give George clear air for the best possible exit and braking performance.

"With these cars, you cannot follow at a two-tenths gap. Ferrari’s best chance was to gain momentum from the final corner or attack very late under braking. George’s defence was extremely impressive.

"You might not have given him even a 50 per cent chance of keeping both Ferraris behind; the virtual safety car helped cool the situation for a lap or two and allowed him to manage his energy, but he executed the defence superbly."

title: Alex Palou equals all-time record after winning fifth IndyCar title in dominant fashion
excerpt:
Alex Palou has become just the second driver to win the US open-wheel national racing championship four times successively after clinching his fifth IndyCar crown.

The Chip Ganassi Racing star clinched the title with a race to spare with a fifth-place at the Milwaukee Mile's second race of a double-header, which was technically Race 1, with the first of the two races being postponed from Saturday due to rain and then completed on Sunday, following Race 2, where Palou took 10th.

His nearest challenger, Kyle Kirkwood failed to win and score the necessary points to set up a Laguna Seca finale shootout, leaving the Spanish racer to collect a fifth IndyCar title in just six seasons.

Since joining CGR in his second season in 2021, Palou has only failed to win the title in 2022, when he finished fifth as Will Power took a second title.

Palou has now moved to third on the all-time titles list, behind A.J Foyt on seven and outgoing CGR team-mate Scott Dixon, who is bringing to an end a near quarter-century stay in the #9 car to join McLaren from next season.

Palou had been level with Mario Andretti, Sebastien Bourdais, and Dario Franchitti in the four-time climb, but now stands alone as a quintuple champion.

In winning the 2023, 2024, 2025, and 2026 titles successively, Palou has also equalled Bourdais' record for successive US open-wheel national racing titles.

The Frenchman claimed the 2004-2007 titles under the 'Champ Car World Series' banner, which had been born out of the old CART series.

Reunification following the split happened in 2008, with the most successive titles in the 'IndyCar' era since, being Franchitti's three in a row between 2009-2011, which Palou has now beaten.

title: Red Bull has 'good chemistry' as Laurent Mekies and Max Verstappen continue rebuild
excerpt:
David Coulthard believes Laurent Mekies and Max Verstappen share "good chemistry" as the pair continue to rebuild the team following a period of transition.

Since 2024, Red Bull has lost Christian Horner, Adrian Newey, Jonathan Wheatley, Will Courtenay, Craig Skinner, and Helmut Marko from their respective positions as team principal, chief technical officer, sporting director, head of strategy, chief designer, and driver advisor, with Gianpiero Lambiase also set to leave as head of race engineering and Verstappen's engineer to join McLaren.

Following Horner's sacking in July 2025, Red Bull GmbH drafted in Mekies from sister team Racing Bulls to replace the Briton, with Frenchman Mekies having previously worked for the FIA as safety director and deputy race director.

He also enjoyed a spell at Ferrari as sporting and racing director before moving to Racing Bulls in 2024 as team principal, before the call to replace Horner last July.

Under his stewardship, Verstappen launched a late-season bid for the 2025 title, missing out by just two points, and steered the Red Bull Powertrains project through its final stages before the in-house engine debuted in 2026.

Red Bull has also captured Gwen Lagrue from Mercedes to assume control of the junior programme, with Mekies also agreeing to a new contract with Verstappen until 2030 to finally end the swirling rumours about the Dutchman leaving.

Speaking about the atmosphere at his former team, which he raced for between 2005 and 2008 and remains an ambassador for, Coulthard spoke of the "good chemistry" between team principal and driver.

"Laurent's job is to make sure that they have the right people growing within, and the right people coming in," Coulthard exclusively told RacingNews365.

"Max is someone who brings people, so it's like an Adrian Newey; if Adrian is there, people think: 'Oh, he must know', and you can see that it hasn't worked out, but in the longer term, I'm sure they'll come forward.

"It takes time to build, but I think the key thing is that Laurent was part of the Red Bull family, so he hasn't had to build that relationship with Austria and the owners because they know him already.

"He brings a wealth of experience from the FIA, from Ferrari, from his career, and he's a different personality and has a different way of operating than Christian Horner, but there's more than one person who wins a world championship as a team principal.

"I think Laurent understands that; he's very calm, and he understands that Max has the right to be frustrated, because he understands the team is frustrated.

"The chemistry is good, and I think that helps take away the doubt from the media, which then adds to the chemistry."

title: Lando Norris wielding new 'power and influence' at McLaren
excerpt:
Lando Norris has explained how he is using the "power and influence" he has discovered he has at McLaren as the team looks to get back in the title fight.

After an initial poor start to their title defences, Norris and McLaren have been name-checked by points leader Kimi Antonelli as the new fastest team following wins in Hungary and in the Netherlands.

Norris has moved to within 83 points of Antonelli as talk of a Max Verstappen-esque 2025-style comeback has been raised.

Norris believes that he is driving better than in his championship-winning year and is growing into his status as a world champion, and the responsibilities this has within the team.

Speaking after signing a new long-term contract to stay with McLaren until 2030 and extend his stay into a third decade, Norris has explained how, now he has the weight and experience behind him, he is wielding the "power and influence I have over the directions we work in as a team."

"You learn over the years when you should talk, when you shouldn't," Norris told Sky Sports.

"In terms of how much power you have as the driver and as an individual, in the first few years, you're not going to overstep any mark. I'm certainly not going to raise my voice above someone else, kind of thing.

"With time, you learn that my role is not simply just driving the car. It's also how can I be a leader, how can I lead the team, how can I be a voice for all the people that work here, all the guys and girls? How can I push them to do better, to be better? As well as pushing myself, of course. And how can we all work and do that as a team?

"I've just learned the power that I can have and influence I can have over the directions that we work in as a team. Of course, I never want to abuse that, but at the same time, I know that I'm in a position where I can be forceful to try and get what I want, from a car, from the team, from people around me.

"And that's a very important thing. You've got to utilise that, I think, as an athlete, no matter what sport you're in. You've got to know how to try and get what you want as an individual.

"And I feel like I'm in a very good place right now with the people I have around me, my team, people we have in different positions, team leaders, all of those things, and the work ethic of the whole team, which is really the most important thing at the end of the day."

title: Lewis Hamilton is hoping Ferrari 'turn up the heat' in Mercedes title pursuit
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton believes Ferrari must "turn up the heat" on Mercedes in the F1 title fight heading to its home Italian Grand Prix.

After 12 rounds of the season, Hamilton is in third in the drivers' standings, 59 points behind championship leader Kimi Antonelli, but level with his Mercedes team-mate George Russell on 183 points, although Russell is ahead by dint of having two wins to Hamilton's one.

Ferrari is 87 points behind Mercedes in the constructors' championship, and has two wins to the Brackley squad's eight, with McLaren also increasingly resurgent, with Lando Norris having won the previous two races in Hungary and the Netherlands.

Hamilton has claimed only one podium in the five races following his win in Barcelona, through a mix of penalties and Ferrari not extracting the maximum from its car, with the SF-26 not entirely expected to suit Monza.

Owing to the small turbo design, the Ferrari engine is stronger at tight, twisty circuits and on initial throttle application, but not at top-end straight line speed.

However, Hamilton believes Ferrari must "turn up the heat" on his former team to beat them to the titles.

"We've obviously got a lot of work to do to try to close the gap to those Mercedes cars," Hamilton told media, including RacingNews365.

"We're in a much different place [heading to Monza] than we have been in the past, obviously last year.

"We're still second in the constructors' championship. We've got a lot of positives to take from this first half of the season.

"In the next [races], we really need to turn up the heat if we're going to have any chance to beat these guys."
